bio: I'm a backend engineer who makes complex data systems reliable. I spent two years at Gainsight as the de facto lead on Unification, a master data management platform serving 1,000+ enterprise customers and 60M+ records, then did a fintech co-op at Hometap building underwriting and valuation services.

Outside work, I build performance-critical systems: a C++ matching engine at 5.2 µs median latency, and Clearline, an event-driven trade settlement engine in Go, Kafka, and Postgres. I'm finishing my MS in Software Engineering Systems at Northeastern in December 2026.

Refactored legacy risk valuation code using AI tools (Claude, Cursor), reviewing every change; caught an AI-generated defect that returned 500 errors from a downstream API before it shipped.
Added audit logging and event tracking across backend API endpoints.

Owned Unification end to end as de facto lead: a multi-tenant master data management platform that merged customer records from many source systems into one source of truth for 1,000+ enterprise customers and 60M+ records. Other teams built their features on it.
Turned enterprise customer requests into features with the PM, from design docs reviewed by architects through launch and production support.

Improved ID resolution with hashing and encoding to match duplicate records across sources.

Scaled Java Spring Boot services with multithreading and asynchronous processing.
Owned observability: Sumo Logic alerts routed to Slack, Grafana dashboards, incident triage.
Mentored a new hire; reviewed code; wrote JUnit tests run in CI.

clearline.title: Clearline
clearline.tagline: Event-driven trade settlement and double-entry ledger engine
clearline.summary: Orders arrive through a REST API, are matched by a C++ matching engine, settled into a Postgres double-entry ledger exactly once, and reflected in a live balance cache and dashboard.
clearline.architectureNote: A reconciler continuously verifies the books balance and the cache matches the ledger.
engineering: Exactly-once effect on at-least-once Kafka: idempotent consumers, offsets committed after the DB commit, and a transactional outbox (no dual writes).
Two-layer order idempotency: Valkey response cache with compare-and-set Lua scripts plus deterministic order IDs deduped in the matcher.
Deterministic recovery: the in-memory C++ engine replays the Kafka orders log; trade IDs come from Kafka offsets, so replays are byte-identical and downstream dedupe absorbs them.
Failure handling: exponential backoff with jitter, classified errors, a dead-letter queue with a replay tool, single-active-leader outbox relay via Postgres advisory lock.
Money as NUMERIC(20,8) end to end; append-only ledger enforced by DB triggers; BigInt fixed point in the browser.
Prometheus metrics on every service, latency measured via timestamps in Kafka headers, Kafka consumer lag collector, 6 alerts unit-tested with promtool.
clearline.resultsContext: Apple M4 (4P+6E), 16 GB, macOS, whole stack in Docker Desktop with the load generator on the same machine; full durability (Kafka acks=all on a single broker, Postgres synchronous_commit and fsync on, Valkey appendfsync=always); open-loop load, 30 s per rate, 0 request errors.
results: Throughput scaled 20x: 100 trades/s baseline, then 731 trades/s (batched, per-partition-concurrent cache updates), then 2,000 trades/s (plus set-based batched settlement). 2,000 was the highest rate offered, so capacity was not reached.
p99 order-to-ledger under 150 ms at every measured rate up to 2,000 trades/s; p50 12.7 ms at 2,000 trades/s.
p99 at 250 trades/s: 129 ms to 23 ms (5.6x lower). Cache freshness p99: 4.8 s to 94 ms.
Correctness: 0 double-postings across 992 duplicate deliveries from 8 concurrent workers, checked against an independent oracle.

projects.subtitle: LowLatencyBuffer
points: Lock-free single-producer/single-consumer queue with cache-line isolation: 5.2 µs P50 submit-to-book (Apple M4).
Custom slab allocator with zero heap allocation on the hot path; resolved a producer/consumer deadlock.
Price-time priority matching engine with O(1) insert/cancel/lookup: 1.1 to 1.6 µs per order-book operation.
Profiled cross-core cache handoff on the M4 at about 1 µs, showing the remaining latency floor was OS scheduler jitter, not the code.
Now powers Clearline's matching engine over gRPC.
